job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the community bank on Main Street in Springfield, Ohio by quarter to nine. I'm a credit analyst trainee, so I review small-business and car loan applications, call people when something's missing and write up a recommendation for the loan officer. I spend about an hour a day with an AI assistant, mostly tidying my write-ups, and I check every word. On Wednesdays I sing in the church choir, and the rest of the week I'm planning a wedding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get the job, and who's the wedding with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied finance at a state university with a good result, and I did a summer as a teller at this same bank. They hired me back. My fiancé, Daniel, is a third-year electrician apprentice, and we share a rented duplex with my cousin Rania. My parents run a small bakery, so money isn't loose, but they'd help in an emergency, and I owe about 11 thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say AI is a decent assistant and no more. I'd tell the choir people that we've heard all this before, and it will find its place like online banking did. Online I'd probably not say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine in my job, but I worry about the bank. Our branch count has already dropped twice in the last three years, and a bigger bank might buy us. That's the thing that keeps me up, more than software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, learn the lending side properly, and aim to be a loan officer within three years. I'd put 200 a month aside for the wedding and our first place. I'd also keep using the assistant for tidying, but not for decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mainly about the bank being sold. Otherwise it's the normal life I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bigger bank might buy yours. What happens to you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably merge the back office and keep a smaller front desk. I'd either move to a bigger city or lose my job. Daniel's apprenticeship ties us here, so I'd hope for a post in Columbus and a long drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about using the assistant at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, as long as it's me signing off. I trust people more than the tool, but a tool that fixes my commas is a help. My mum says a tool is like a good oven, you still have to know how to bake.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent assistant** and no more.
I'd tell the choir we've heard all this before, and it will find its place like **online banking**.
think: I'm fine in my job, but I worry about the **bank** being sold.
The branch count has already **dropped twice** in three years.
do: Learn the **lending side** and aim to be a loan officer in three years.
Put **200 a month** aside for the wedding and our first place.
Use the assistant for **tidying**, not decisions.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mainly about the bank being sold.
S0.quote: My mum says a tool is like a good oven, you still have to know how to bake.
fieldNote: Beth's unease is about **bank consolidation**, not AI.
Daniel's apprenticeship ties the couple to town, limiting her options.
Her mother's oven comparison shows how she thinks about tools.

steps.text: Learn the lending side and aim for loan officer within three years
Put 200 a month into the wedding and first-home savings
Use the assistant to tidy write-ups, but never for decisions
Book the wedding venue with Daniel for next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use the tools but keep a person who explains decisions to customers. At church I'd say we should watch out for the people who aren't comfortable with technology, especially older folks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of what I do, reading applications, checking numbers and writing the summary, could be done by software. The relationship part stays with people. But the bank will want fewer juniors if it can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better with the tools, to be the person who checks them. I'd also move toward the customer side, meeting small-business owners and learning what their shops need. I'd save 300 a month and ask the bank about a lending certificate course, since it would make me harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. But I have Daniel's steady trade income on the side, so I'm not on a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel's income makes it less of a cliff. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'll earn good money once he finishes in two years, and electricians are needed everywhere. It's a hands-on job, and I do think it will last longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a customer who got refused by a machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a person here to explain it, and I'd look at their case again. People want to be heard, even when the answer's no.

say: I'd say use the tools but keep a **person** who explains decisions to customers.
I'd say we should watch out for **older folks** who aren't comfortable with technology.
think: Reading applications and writing summaries could be done by **software**.
The **relationship part** stays with people, but the bank will want fewer juniors.
do: Learn the tools well enough to be the person who **checks** them.
Move toward **small-business** customers and learn what their shops need.
Save **300 a month** and take a lending certificate course.
feel: **Anxious**, a bit, but not on a cliff edge with Daniel's trade income.
S1.quote: People want to be heard, even when the answer's no.
fieldNote: Beth's anxiety is cushioned by her **fiancé's trade**, which she thinks will last longer.
She values the human voice in lending, a central part of her identity.
Plans to become the checker of the tools, a steady, moderate step.

steps.text: Learn the bank's AI tools well enough to check their output
Enrol in the lending certificate course the bank offers
Save 300 a month toward the wedding and first home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask the bank's president what the plan is, and I'd ask directly. At church I'd say we need to look out for each other. I'd tell Daniel and my parents that night, and we'd sit down with a paper and write out our options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone in two years or turns into something very different. The numbers part is what the machine does best. I'd be thinking about how much the bank can keep people on before the owners sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone and pay down the card first. I'd push the wedding to something small, a church hall and a family meal. I'd ask my parents if I can do shifts at the bakery, because it's hands-on and a bakery will be there for a few more years. And I'd see whether the bank would keep me on the customer desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be scared, but I'd also be steadier than I'd expect, because I'd have Daniel and the family around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small wedding. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be a bit sad, because I've always imagined a big one. But a wedding is a day and a marriage is a life, and I'd rather start on solid ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the thing you most need in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere safe to work for the next three years, and someone to tell me honestly what's coming. I can handle bad news if it's clear.

say: I'd ask the bank's **president** what the plan is.
At church I'd say we need to **look out** for each other.
think: My job is gone in two years or becomes something **very different**.
I'd wonder how long the bank can keep people on before the **owners sell**.
do: Cut spending to the bone and pay down the **card** first.
Scale the wedding to a **church hall** and a family meal.
Ask my parents for **shifts at the bakery** and ask the bank about the customer desk.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier than expected with Daniel and family around.
S2.quote: A wedding is a day and a marriage is a life, and I'd rather start on solid ground.
fieldNote: Beth's fear is **real**, but family and faith steady her.
The small wedding is a clear trade-off she accepts.
Her request is for honest news, even if it's bad.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills, and pay down the card first
Hold the savings in a plain account for six months of cover
Shrink the wedding to a church hall and family meal
Ask my parents for shifts at their bakery while the bank decides

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough time to prepare and that we should start training early. At church I'd say that families and congregations should be ready to help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy, but not anxious. In five years I'd be 27, probably married with a first child, and Daniel would be a full electrician. A household with a trade in it is a steadier one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the lending certificate and aim to be a loan officer who works with small businesses, because people still need a human there. I'd save 350 a month, and plan the wedding at a normal size. I'd also keep up with the tools, since the bank will expect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing weather forecasts for a year ahead, and getting on with the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a household with a trade in it is steadier. Do you rely on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Wiring and repair work is needed even in hard times. If the bank let me go, we could manage on Daniel's pay for a while, though not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be honest about the plan and pay for training. If they said it was happening, I'd give them my best effort. If they hid it, I'd start looking.

say: I'd say five years is enough time to **prepare**, so let's train early.
At church I'd say congregations should be ready to **help** each other.
think: I'd be uneasy, not anxious, as I'd be **27** and probably a mother.
A household with a **trade** in it is a steadier one.
do: Finish the **lending certificate** and aim to be a small-business loan officer.
Save **350 a month** and hold a normal-sized wedding.
Keep up with the **tools** since the bank will expect it.
feel: **Uneasy**, like hearing a long weather forecast and getting on with the day.
S3.quote: A household with a trade in it is a steadier one.
fieldNote: Beth's steadiness comes from **Daniel's electrician trade**.
She treats honesty from employers as the thing that earns her effort.
She imagines motherhood on the timeline.

steps.text: Finish the lending certificate within two years
Save 350 a month for the wedding and first home
Hold a normal-sized wedding and plan a first child
Keep using the assistant and take the bank's training days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so let's use it. At work I'd train newer staff, and at church I'd say we should teach the young to work hard and be kind. I'd stay positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, maybe a mother of two, with a house and a steady career at a bank or a credit union. I'd keep learning, but there's enough time that nothing needs to be rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work up to loan officer, then branch manager if the branch exists. I'd save 300 a month and buy a small house with Daniel within five years. I'd also volunteer at the church's money-advice night, which helps people with budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and thankful. It's the world where I get to build the life I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would there be anything in this world that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the changes all came at once at the end. Ten years can feel like plenty, and then suddenly it's two. I'd keep checking in with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the money-advice night. What would you do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help people write out a budget and understand a loan. A lot of folks are scared of the paperwork, and a calm explanation goes a long way.

say: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so **let's use it**.
At church I'd say we should teach the young to **work hard** and be kind.
think: I'd feel calm: **32**, maybe a mother of two, with a house and steady career.
There's enough time that **nothing needs rushing**.
do: Work up to **loan officer**, then branch manager if the branch exists.
Save **300 a month** and buy a small house with Daniel.
feel: **Calm** and thankful, building the life I planned.
S4.quote: Ten years can feel like plenty, and then suddenly it's two.
fieldNote: Beth's calm comes from **time and faith**.
She guards against complacency in her own words.
Her volunteering fits the wish to help people understand loans.

steps.text: Work up to loan officer, then branch manager
Save 300 a month and buy a small house within five years
Start a family with Daniel after the house
Volunteer at the church money-advice night each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the wedding and the first baby would land right in the middle of it. What would help is a community that pulls together, banks and churches that look after their own, and Daniel's trade staying in demand. Also, a bit of honesty from the big firms would go a long way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I want my work to be for. I got into community banking because I like helping a family get its first loan. If a machine decides, I'd like a person at least to explain it to them.

headlineQuote: I got into community banking because I like helping a family get its first loan.
portrait: Beth, 22, is a **credit analyst trainee** at a community bank in Springfield, Ohio.
She shares a duplex with her fiancé Daniel, an **electrician apprentice**, and her cousin Rania.
Traditional and steady, she uses an AI assistant a little and **checks every word**.
She moves from uneasy to **anxious** at two years, steadied by Daniel's trade and her church.
Her deepest wish is for a **person** to explain loan decisions to customers.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because the wedding and a first baby would land in the middle of it.
whatWouldHelp: A community that pulls together, honest news from big firms and Daniel's **trade** staying in demand.
